From what y'all said in lab 05 (summarized): Creative ways to use GenAI: - Feedback on visualizations - AI as grader or critical reviewer (Catching duplicated work across teammates; jargon-only proofread; grader primed with your past feedback) - AI as a naive audience (Explain it back to me.) - Debugging and code cleanup (AI-generated edge cases to stress-test code, like how cutoff values would be handled) - Brainstorming analyses - Challenging conclusions: Alternative explanations, limitations, confounders, counterarguments. - Report structure and flow - Finding sources or background - explaining concepts like sensitivity and specificity (mock debate on sensitivity vs. specificity) - team planning and dividing tasks - and generating test data for code Note: Telling AI to use Socratic mode How to NOT use GenAI: - Having AI write the report, analysis or conclusions - Copying code they don’t understand - Made-up data, results or citations - Having AI do the whole project or a whole section - Letting AI make the decisions - Having AI build the visualizations from scratch - Having AI make the general-audience piece - Not disclosing AI use - Not uploading the CS01 data to an AI tool ::: ## Course Announcements **Due Dates**: - **Lab 06** due Fri (11:59 PM) - 📄 **Final Project Proposal** due Sun (11:59 PM) - 🔘 Lecture Participation survey "due" after class Notes: - My office hours moved from today to Fri at 11AM (this week only) - Either ** work from lab06 data** or et the data in RStudio for today (and `install.packages()` `"OCSdata"`, `"skimr"`, `"GGally"`, and `"corrplot"`). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("OCSdata") # OCSdata::raw_data("ocs-bp-air-pollution", outpath = getwd()) # once CS02 repos are created (after proposals are due 11/8), the file will also be at "data/pm25_data.csv" in your repo pm <- read_csv("OCS_data/data/raw/pm25_data.csv") ``` ::: # Question {background-color="#92A86A"} > With what accuracy can we predict US annual average air pollution concentrations? # Wrangling {background-color="#92A86A"} ## Viewing the data Take a look... . . . [ What's something you've learned about the data from the skimr output?]{style="background-color: #ADD8E6"} . . . Things to note: ::: incremental - data are summarized by variable type - `empty`/`n_missing` gives you a sense of how much data are missing for each variable - `n_unique` for `state` indicates that we have data for 49 states - many different distributions for continuous data, but many show bimodal distribution - large range of possible values for many variables (i.e. population) ::: . . . - Consider variable type - need more factors? - Check how monitors are spread across states and cities: which places are overrepresented? decide what to do - log or other transformations necessary? decide during EDA ## Why 49 "states"? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> distinct(state) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 49 × 1 state 1 Alabama 2 Arizona 3 Arkansas 4 California 5 Colorado 6 Connecticut 7 Delaware 8 District Of Columbia 9 Florida 10 Georgia # ℹ 39 more rows ``` ::: ::: - DC is included - Alaska and Hawaii are not ## Where are the monitors? {.scrollable} [ Guess: how many monitors does San Diego County have?]{style="background-color: #ADD8E6"} . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> filter(county == "San Diego") |> select(city, county, county_pop, popdens_county, value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 5 city county county_pop popdens_county value 1 Chula Vista San Diego 3095313 284. 12.3 2 El Cajon San Diego 3095313 284. 13.4 3 San Diego San Diego 3095313 284. 11.3 4 Escondido San Diego 3095313 284. 17.5 5 San Diego San Diego 3095313 284. 13.7 6 Boulevard San Diego 3095313 284. 3.47 ``` ::: ::: . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> filter(city == "Baltimore") |> select(city, county, county_pop, popdens_county, value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 5 city county county_pop popdens_county value 1 Baltimore Baltimore (City) 620961 2962. 12.2 2 Baltimore Baltimore (City) 620961 2962. 12.5 3 Baltimore Baltimore (City) 620961 2962. 12.8 4 Baltimore Baltimore (City) 620961 2962. 14.3 5 Baltimore Baltimore (City) 620961 2962. 13.3 ``` ::: ::: . . . San Diego County has 6 monitors for about 3.1 million people. Baltimore, a city that is its own (small) county, has 5 monitors for about 621,000 people. Monitor placement doesn't simply follow population. . . . And not every monitor is in a city: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> count(city, sort = TRUE) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 city n 1 Not in a city 103 2 New York 9 3 Cleveland 6 4 Baltimore 5 5 Chicago 5 ``` ::: ::: ## The outcome: `value` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> ggplot(aes(x = value)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#2b6a99", color = "white") + labs(x = "Annual average PM2.5 in 2008 (ug/m^3)", y = "Number of monitors") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: . . . Which states have the highest averages? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> group_by(state) |> summarize(n_monitors = n(), mean_pm25 = mean(value)) |> arrange(desc(mean_pm25)) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 3 state n_monitors mean_pm25 1 West Virginia 14 13.4 2 Ohio 44 12.9 3 Pennsylvania 32 12.8 4 Georgia 28 12.5 5 Indiana 36 12.4 ``` ::: ::: ## How many monitors exceed health guidelines? {.scrollable} [ Guess: what share of these monitors would exceed today's EPA annual standard (9 ug/m^3^)?]{style="background-color: #ADD8E6"} . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> summarize( epa_2008 = sum(value > 15), who_2005 = sum(value > 10), epa_2024 = sum(value > 9), who_2021 = sum(value > 5) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 epa_2008 who_2005 epa_2024 who_2021 1 28 583 686 864 ``` ::: ::: . . . Of 876 monitors, 28 (3%) were above the EPA standard in effect in 2008 (15 ug/m^3^). By today's EPA standard (9 ug/m^3^), 686 (78%) would be. By WHO's current guideline (5 ug/m^3^), 864 (99%). ::: aside A rough comparison: EPA's official test uses a 3-year average, and these are 2008 values, not today's air. ::: ## Feature Correlation On Friday, you looked for variables that seemed **redundant**. Let's check. Why do we care if variables in our dataset are correlated? - we don't want to include redundant variables - can add unnecessary noise to our algorithm causing a reduction in prediction accuracy - can cause our algorithm to be slower - can also make it difficult to interpret what variables are actually predictive ## Which features track the outcome? [ Guess: which feature is most correlated with `value`?]{style="background-color: #ADD8E6"} . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> select(where(is.numeric)) |> cor() |> as_tibble(rownames = "feature") |> select(feature, r = value) |> filter(feature != "value") |> slice_max(abs(r), n = 10) |> ggplot(aes(x = r, y = fct_reorder(feature, r))) + geom_col(fill = "#2b6a99") + labs(x = "Correlation with value (r)", y = NULL, title = "Top 10 features") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: . . . - `CMAQ` (the chemical model) is the strongest, followed by emissions (`nei`), roads (`prisec`), and the satellite measure (`aod`) - These are moderate correlations: no single feature predicts PM~2.5~ on its own ## Correlations among features ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} PM_cor <- cor(pm |> select(where(is.numeric))) ``` ::: ::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"} Taking a look at all of our numeric variables... ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot::corrplot(PM_cor, tl.cex = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: - deep blue \| strongly, positively correlated - deep red \| strongly, negatively correlated If we don't care about direction, but only strength...*and* using [hierarchical clustering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hierarchical_clustering): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} corrplot::corrplot(abs(PM_cor), order = "hclust", tl.cex = 0.5, col.lim = c(0, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: ::: Observations: - development variables (`imp`), road density (`pri`), and the emission (`nei`) variables all seem to be correlated with their group - several predictors are moderately correlated with `value` (our outcome), but none strongly ## Development (`imp`) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} select(pm, contains("imp")) |> GGally::ggpairs() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: . . . The same measure at different radii is strongly correlated with itself. The emissions (`nei`) and road (`pri`) groups show the same pattern (see the notes). ::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"} ### Emissions (`nei`) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} select(pm, contains("nei")) |> GGally::ggpairs() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: ### Road Density (`pri`) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} select(pm, contains("pri")) |> GGally::ggcorr(hjust = .85, size = 3, layout.exp = 2, label = TRUE, # same colors as corrplot above: blue = positive, red = negative low = "#67001F", mid = "#F7F7F7", high = "#053061") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: ::: ## Are the categories correlated with one another? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> select(log_nei_2008_pm25_sum_10000, popdens_county, log_pri_length_10000, imp_a10000, county_pop) |> GGally::ggpairs() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: . . . Reminder: - **log_nei_2008_pm25_sum_10000** \| Tons of emissions from major sources database (annual data) sum of all sources within a circle with a radius of 10000 meters of distance around the monitor (Natural log)\ - **popdens_county** \| Population density (number of people per kilometer squared area of the county) - **log_pri_length_10000** \| Count of primary road length in meters in a circle with a radius of 10000 meters around the monitor (Natural log)
-- Highways only\ - **imp_a10000** \| Impervious surface measure
-- Within a circle with a radius of 10000 meters around the monitor\ - **county_pop** \| Population of the county of the monitor ## Log-transforming right-skewed data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pm |> mutate(log_popdens_county=log(popdens_county), log_pop_county = log(county_pop)) |> select(log_nei_2008_pm25_sum_10000, log_popdens_county, log_pri_length_10000, imp_a10000, log_pop_county) |> GGally::ggpairs() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](11-cs02-eda_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=2100} ::: ::: ## Your Turn {.scrollable} [ Try to learn at least three things about the data that we haven't yet discussed now on your own.]{style="background-color: #ADD8E6"} ::: aside Put a [green]{.sticky-green} sticky on the front of your computer when you're done.
